  - *Throwing:* Shaping clay symmetrically on a rotating **potter's wheel**.
  - *Stages of Clay Dryness:*
    - **Plastic State:** Wet, soft, moldable.
    - **Leather-Hard State:** Partially dried, firm like cheese; ideal for carving patterns, trimming foot rings, and attaching handles with **slip** (liquid clay glue).
    - **Bone-Dry / Greenware:** Completely air-dried, fragile, ready for the first firing.
    - **Bisque / Biscuit Firing:** First firing in a kiln at $900^\circ - 1,000^\circ\text{C}$ to vitrify clay into porous permanent ceramic.
    - **Glazing & Glaze Firing:** Applying powdered silica and metallic oxides, then refiring at high temperature to form an impervious, glossy glass coating.

---

topics.title: Graphics, Printmaking, and Textiles
topics.content:
- **Typography and Graphic Design:**
  - *Serif Fonts:* Characters having small decorative finishing strokes / feet at the ends of letters (e.g., Times New Roman).
  - *Sans-Serif Fonts:* Clean, modern characters without decorative finishing feet (e.g., Arial, Helvetica).
  - *Calligraphy:* The art of beautiful, expressive hand lettering using broad-edged pens or brushes.
- **Printmaking Methods:**
  - *Relief Printing:* The raised surface carries the ink; the non-image areas are carved away (e.g., **Woodcut, Linocut**).
  - *Intaglio Printing:* The design is incised or etched into metal plates below the surface; ink is forced into grooves (e.g., **Etching, Engraving**).
  - *Serigraphy (Screen Printing):* Stencil printmaking using a fine mesh screen (silk/polyester) stretched on a wooden frame; ink is pressed through open mesh areas using a rubber **squeegee**.
- **Textile Crafts:**
  - *Tie and Dye (Adire Oniko):* Fabric is tied with raffia or string, folded, or pleated before dipping into an indigo dye bath.
  - *Batik:* Fabric is painted or stamped with **melted wax** (resist), dyed in cold water dye, and boiled to remove wax.
  - *Adire Eleko:* Traditional Yoruba paste-resist textile using **cassava starch paste (*lafun*)** painted through stencils or freehand with feathers onto fabric.
  - *Weaving:* Interlacing two sets of threads at right angles: **Warp** (longitudinal lengthwise threads held in tension) and **Weft / Woof** (transverse crosswise threads woven across). Examples: **Aso-Oke** (Yoruba narrow strip loom) and **Akwete** (Igbo broad vertical loom).

---

# SECTION 3: TRADITIONAL AFRICAN ART HISTORY

topics.title: Classical Nigerian Art Traditions
topics.content:
- **The Nok Culture (c. 900 BC – 200 AD):**
  - Oldest terracotta sculptures in Sub-Saharan Africa, discovered near Nok village in Kaduna State.
  - **Key Diagnostic Traits:**
    - Distinct **triangular or oval pierced eyes, pupils, nostrils, and ears**.
    - Flared nostrils, open expressive lips.
    - Elaborate braided, tiered, and beaded coiffures.
    - Broken hollow terracotta figures depicting human heads, monkeys, and elephants.
- **Igbo-Ukwu (9th Century AD):**
  - Located in Anambra State; excavated by British archaeologist **Thurstan Shaw** in 1959.
  - **Key Diagnostic Traits:**
    - High-level metallurgy: sophisticated leaded bronze casting using cire-perdue.
    - Masterpiece: **The Roped Bronze Pot** (a vessel enclosed within a delicate netting of simulated rope).
    - Ornate surface decoration featuring geometric bands, spirals, insects (crickets, flies, beetles), and snakes.
    - Over 165,000 glass beads, ivory tusks, and regalia associated with the sacred **Eze Nri** monarchy.
- **Ile-Ife Art (11th – 15th Century):**
  - Classical Yoruba art centered around the spiritual home of the Ooni.
  - **Key Diagnostic Traits:**
    - Supreme **idealized naturalism / realism** with serene facial composure.
    - Lifelike proportions of the human face.
    - **Delicate parallel vertical striations (scarification lines)** running down the cheeks and forehead.
    - Holes around the hairline, chin, and lower jaw used to attach real hair beards and beaded crowns.
    - Media: Terracotta and brass/copper alloy heads (*cire-perdue*). Famous masterpiece: The **Olokun Head**.
- **Benin Court Art (14th – 19th Century):**
  - Royal court art made exclusively for the palace of the **Oba of Benin** by the hereditary royal brass-casters guild (**Iguneronmwon**).
  - **Key Diagnostic Traits:**
    - Commemorative portrait brass heads of deceased Obas placed on royal ancestral altars.
    - Stylized depiction with large eyes, heavy features, and **beaded high coral collars (*odigba*)** extending from neck up to the lower lip.
    - Retangular bronze relief plaques depicting warriors, Portuguese soldiers, and court ceremonies that once lined wooden pillars of the palace.
    - **The 16th-Century Ivory Pendant Mask of Queen Mother Idia:** Worn at the waist of the Oba; carved with miniature Portuguese heads and mudfish along the tiara; adopted as the official emblem of **FESTAC '77**.
- **Esie Soapstone Carvings (Kwara State):**
  - Discovered in 1933; the largest collection of stone sculptures in Africa (over 800 figures carved from soft **steatite / soapstone**), depicting seated men and women playing instruments and holding weapons.

---

# SECTION 4: MODERN & CONTEMPORARY NIGERIAN ART

topics.title: Pioneers and the Zaria Art Society
topics.content:
- **Pioneers of Modern Nigerian Art:**
  - **Aina Onabolu (1882–1963):** Universally acknowledged as the **"Father of Modern Nigerian Art"**. Self-taught portraitist who proved that Africans could master European perspective, anatomy, and academic realism without white supervision. Successfully lobbied the colonial administration to introduce formal art education into Nigerian secondary schools, becoming the first indigenous art master at King's College, Lagos.
  - **Akinola Lasekan (1916–1972):** Pioneer portrait painter and renowned political cartoonist for Nnamdi Azikiwe's *West African Pilot*, using art as a potent ideological weapon against colonial oppression.
  - **Chief Justus Akeredolu:** Pioneered miniature realistic **thorn carvings** using wild cotton-tree thorns in Nigeria.
- **The Zaria Art Society ("The Zaria Rebels", 1958):**
  - Formed in 1958 by student artists at the Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology (now ABU, Zaria) in protest against Eurocentric academic curricula.
  - Key Founders: **Uche Okeke, Bruce Onobrakpeya, Demas Nwoko, Yusuf Grillo, Simon Okeke, Felix Ekeada, and Oseloka Osadebe**.
  - **Core Ideology: "Natural Synthesis":** The conscious, deliberate fusion of the best elements of traditional Nigerian cultural heritage, folklore, and materials with valid Western technical methods, rejecting slavish imitation of European styles.
- **Contemporary Nigerian Masters:**
  - **Ben Enwonwu (1917–1994):** Celebrated painter and sculptor; merged African aesthetics with Western technique. Commissioned by Queen Elizabeth II to sculpt her bronze portrait (1957). Masterpiece: **"Anyanwu" (The Awakening)** at the National Museum, Lagos; painted the iconic *"Tutu"* portrait series.
  - **Bruce Onobrakpeya (b. 1932):** Master printmaker, painter, and sculptor; pioneer of **Plastography** (printmaking using plastic relief surfaces), metal foil relief, and deep etching based on Urhobo folklore and Christian mythology.
  - **Yusuf Grillo (1934–2021):** Master painter; renowned for stylized, elongated figures depicted in cool harmonic palettes of **deep blues and purples**; celebrated for stained glass and mosaic murals.
  - **Demas Nwoko (b. 1935):** Architect, sculptor, and theater designer; pioneer of "New Culture" architecture utilizing local laterite and terracotta bricks.
  - **Uche Okeke (1933–2016):** Master artist who pioneered the modern aesthetic adaptation of traditional Igbo **Uli** body and wall motifs (delicate, lyrical, minimalist linear designs).

---

name: Music
overview:
**Subject Code:** `MUS`  
**Total Questions in UTME:** 40 Questions  
**Time Target:** 25 – 27 Minutes  
**Maximum Scaled Score:** 100 Marks  
**Authoritative Reference:** Official JAMB IBASS Syllabus for Music  

---

## Overview & How JAMB Tests Music

In the UTME, Music is tested via **40 multiple-choice questions** grouped into four major segments:
1. **Rudiments & Music Theory (~12 Questions):** Clefs, pitch notation, note/rest time values, simple and compound time signatures, accidentals, major/minor scales, intervals (size and quality), and transposition.
2. **Harmony, Part-Writing & Musical Form (~10 Questions):** Triads (root position, 1st and 2nd inversions), primary and secondary triads, cadences (perfect, plagal, imperfect, interrupted), four-part SATB vocal harmony, voice leading rules, and structural forms (Binary, Ternary, Rondo, Sonata-Allegro).
3. **African Music & Organology (~10 Questions):** Characteristics of African music (polyrhythm, call-and-response, syncopation), the Hornbostel-Sachs classification of African traditional musical instruments (Idiophones, Membranophones, Chordophones, Aerophones), and socio-cultural contexts.
4. **Western & Nigerian Music History (~8 Questions):** Eras of Western art music (Baroque, Classical, Romantic) and master composers (Bach, Handel, Mozart, Beethoven), Nigerian art music pioneers (Fela Sowande, T.K.E. Phillips, Akin Euba), and popular music genres (Highlife, Juju, Afrobeat, Fuji).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Distinctions in JAMB Music:**
> - Organological Classifications: **Agogo, Sekere, Ekwe** are **Idiophones**; **Gangan (talking drum), Bata** are **Membranophones**; **Goje, Kora** are **Chordophones**; **Kakaki, Algaita, Oja** are **Aerophones**.
> - Cadences: $V \to I$ is a **Perfect Cadence** (full close); $IV \to I$ is a **Plagal Cadence** ("Amen" cadence); Any chord $\to V$ is an **Imperfect Cadence** (half close); $V \to vi$ is an **Interrupted (Deceptive) Cadence**.
> - Major Scale Semitones: In every major scale, semitones occur strictly between the **3rd–4th** and **7th–8th** degrees.

---

# SECTION 1: RUDIMENTS AND THEORY OF MUSIC

strategies.title: Strategy 1
strategies.description: **Plagal Cadence Recognition:** A cadence moving from **$IV \to I$** is always a **Plagal Cadence**, popularly known as the "Amen Cadence".

strategies.title: Strategy 2
strategies.description: **Order of Sharps and Flats:** Sharps $=$ **FCGDAEB**; Flats $=$ **BEADGCF**. They are exact mirror reversals of each other!

strategies.title: Strategy 3
strategies.description: **Organological Classification of Gangan:** The Yoruba talking drum (*Gangan*) is a **Membranophone**, while the iron gong (*Agogo*) and wooden slit drum (*Ekwe*) are **Idiophones**.

strategies.title: Strategy 4
strategies.description: **Kakaki Instrument Type:** The *Kakaki* is a brass royal trumpet of Northern Nigeria, classified as an **Aerophone**.

strategies.title: Strategy 5
strategies.description: **Major Scale Semitone Locations:** Semitones in a major scale occur strictly between scale degrees **3 and 4**, and **7 and 8**.

strategies.title: Strategy 6
strategies.description: **Compound Duple Time:** **$6/8$** time is **Compound Duple**, meaning it has two main dotted-crotchet beats per bar, NOT six individual beats.

strategies.title: Strategy 7
strategies.description: **Father of Nigerian Church Music:** **T.K.E. Phillips** is the "Father of Nigerian Church Music", while **Fela Sowande** composed the famous *African Suite*.

strategies.title: Strategy 8
strategies.description: **Origin of Fuji Music:** Fuji music evolved from **Were / Ajiwere** Islamic music, created by **Dr. Sikiru Ayinde Barrister**.

strategies.title: Strategy 9
strategies.description: **Rule of Nine for Inverting Intervals:** An interval and its inversion always add up to **$9$**. A Major 3rd inverts to a **Minor 6th** ($3 + 6 = 9$; Major becomes Minor).

strategies.title: Strategy 10
strategies.description: **African Pianism Concept:** The concept of using the European piano as an African percussive drum instrument was pioneered by **Professor Akin Euba**.

topics.title: Notation, Clefs, Notes, and Time Signatures
topics.content:
- **The Stave (Staff) & Clefs:**
  - Standard five horizontal lines and four spaces.
  - **Treble Clef (G Clef):** Loops around the 2nd line ($G_4$). Lines: **E, G, B, D, F**; Spaces: **F, A, C, E**.
  - **Bass Clef (F Clef):** Two dots sandwich the 4th line ($F_3$). Lines: **G, B, D, F, A**; Spaces: **A, C, E, G**.
  - **C Clef (Movable Clef):** Central notch marks Middle C ($C_4$). Placed on 3rd line = **Alto Clef** (used by viola); placed on 4th line = **Tenor Clef** (used by cello, bassoon, trombone).
- **Notes, Rests, and Beat Values:**
  | Note Name | British Name | Relative Duration in Beats (in 4/4 Time) | Equivalent Rest Symbol |
  | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
  | **Whole Note** | **Semibreve** | $4\text{ Beats}$ | Filled bar hanging below 4th line |
  | **Half Note** | **Minim** | $2\text{ Beats}$ | Filled bar resting on 3rd line |
  | **Quarter Note** | **Crotchet** | $1\text{ Beat}$ | Vertical squiggly rest |
  | **Eighth Note** | **Quaver** | $\frac{1}{2}\text{ Beat}$ (Single tail/flag) | Resembles figure '7' with hook |
  | **Sixteenth Note** | **Semiquaver** | $\frac{1}{4}\text{ Beat}$ (Double tail/flag) | Figure '7' with double hooks |
- **Dotted Notes:** A dot placed after a note increases its original duration by **half its value** (e.g., a dotted minim $= 2 + 1 = 3\text{ beats}$; a dotted crotchet $= 1 + \frac{1}{2} = 1\frac{1}{2}\text{ beats}$).
- **Time Signatures:**
  - *Top Number:* Indicates the number of beats per measure/bar.
  - *Bottom Number:* Indicates the type of note receiving one beat ($4 =$ quarter note/crotchet, $8 =$ eighth note/quaver).
  - *Simple Time (Beat unit divides into 2 equal parts):*
    - **Simple Duple:** $\mathbf{2/4}$ ($2$ crotchet beats per bar).
    - **Simple Triple:** $\mathbf{3/4}$ ($3$ crotchet beats per bar).
    - **Simple Quadruple:** $\mathbf{4/4}$ ($4$ crotchet beats per bar; also symbolized as **Common Time, C**).
  - *Compound Time (Beat unit is a dotted note dividing into 3 equal parts):*
    - **Compound Duple:** $\mathbf{6/8}$ ($2$ dotted crotchet beats per bar, counted as two groups of 3 quavers: **1**-2-3, **4**-5-6).
    - **Compound Triple:** $\mathbf{9/8}$ ($3$ dotted crotchet beats per bar).
    - **Compound Quadruple:** $\mathbf{12/8}$ ($4$ dotted crotchet beats per bar).

---

topics.title: Scales, Key Signatures, and Intervals
topics.content:
- **Scale Formulas:**
  - *Major Scale:* Step pattern of **Tone – Tone – Semitone – Tone – Tone – Tone – Semitone** ($T-T-S-T-T-T-S$). Semitones occur between **3–4** and **7–8**.
  - *Natural Minor Scale:* Formula: $T-S-T-T-S-T-T$ (semitones between 2–3 and 5–6).
  - *Harmonic Minor Scale:* Natural minor with the **7th degree raised by a semitone** both ascending and descending (creates an augmented 2nd interval between 6th and 7th degrees).
  - *Melodic Minor Scale:* Raises both **6th and 7th degrees** ascending, but reverts to the natural minor descending.
- **Key Signatures & Order of Accidentals:**
  - **Order of Sharps:** $\mathbf{F^\sharp, C^\sharp, G^\sharp, D^\sharp, A^\sharp, E^\sharp, B^\sharp}$ (*"Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle"*).
    - *Shortcut for Major Keys with Sharps:* The last sharp in the key signature is the **leading note (7th degree)**; raise it by a semitone to find the keynote (e.g., last sharp is $F^\sharp \implies$ Key of G Major).
  - **Order of Flats:** $\mathbf{B^\flat, E^\flat, A^\flat, D^\flat, G^\flat, C^\flat, F^\flat}$ (*"Battle Ends And Down Goes Charles' Father"*).
    - *Shortcut for Major Keys with Flats:* The **penultimate (second to last) flat** is the keynote (e.g., two flats $B^\flat, E^\flat \implies$ Key of $B^\flat$ Major; one flat $B^\flat = \text{Key of F Major}$).
- **Technical Names of Scale Degrees:**
  - 1st: **Tonic** | 2nd: **Supertonic** | 3rd: **Mediant** | 4th: **Subdominant** | 5th: **Dominant** | 6th: **Submediant** | 7th: **Leading Note** | 8th: **Tonic / Octave**.
- **Intervals and Inversions:**
  - Perfect intervals: **Unison, 4th, 5th, Octave**. (Never major or minor!).
  - Major / Minor intervals: **2nd, 3rd, 6th, 7th**.
  - **The Inversion Rule of Nine:**
    $$\text{Original Interval Number} + \text{Inverted Interval Number} = \mathbf{9}$$
    - Perfect becomes **Perfect** (A Perfect 5th inverts to a Perfect 4th).
    - Major becomes **Minor** (A Major 3rd inverts to a Minor 6th).
    - Augmented becomes **Diminished**.

---

# SECTION 2: HARMONY, PART-WRITING AND MUSICAL FORM

topics.title: Triads, Cadences, and Four-Part Harmony
topics.content:
- **Triads and Chord Building:**
  - A triad consists of a **Root, a 3rd, and a 5th**.
  - *Root Position (5/3):* Root is the lowest sounding bass note.
  - *First Inversion (6/3 or 6):* The 3rd of the triad is in the bass.
  - *Second Inversion (6/4):* The 5th of the triad is in the bass.
  - *Primary Triads:* Built on degrees **I (Tonic), IV (Subdominant), and V (Dominant)**; all are major triads in a major key.
- **The Four Musical Cadences (Harmonic Punctuation):**
  1. **Perfect Cadence (Full Close):** Chord $\mathbf{V \to I}$. The ultimate harmonic resolution, sounding like a definitive grammatical period/full stop.
  2. **Plagal Cadence:** Chord $\mathbf{IV \to I}$. Known as the **"Amen" cadence**; traditionally sung at the conclusion of Christian hymns.
  3. **Imperfect Cadence (Half Close):** Any chord ending on the Dominant ($\mathbf{I \to V, ii \to V, IV \to V}$). Sounds unfinished, expectant, like a comma or question mark.
  4. **Interrupted / Deceptive Cadence:** Chord $\mathbf{V \to vi}$. The dominant chord resolves unexpectedly to the minor submediant ($vi$) instead of the expected tonic ($I$), producing a sudden surprise.
- **Part-Writing Rules for SATB (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, Bass):**
  - **Avoid Parallel Fifths and Parallel Octaves:** Two voice parts must never move in parallel motion at the interval of a 5th or an octave.
  - Never allow voice parts to cross (e.g., Tenor singing higher than Alto).

---

topics.title: Musical Terms, Dynamics, and Structural Forms
topics.content:
- **Dynamic Markings:**
  - $pp$ (*Pianissimo* = Very soft) $\to$ $p$ (*Piano* = Soft) $\to$ $mp$ (*Mezzo-piano* = Moderately soft) $\to$ $mf$ (*Mezzo-forte* = Moderately loud) $\to$ $f$ (*Forte* = Loud) $\to$ $ff$ (*Fortissimo* = Very loud).
  - *Crescendo ($<$):* Gradually getting louder; *Decrescendo / Diminuendo ($>$):* Gradually getting softer.
- **Tempo Markings:**
  - *Largo:* Very slow and broad.
  - *Adagio:* Slow, leisurely.
  - *Andante:* At a walking pace.
  - *Allegro:* Quick, lively, fast.
  - *Presto:* Extremely fast.
  - *Accelerando:* Gradually accelerating; *Ritardando / Rallentando:* Gradually slowing down.
- **Structural Musical Forms:**
  - *Binary Form ($AB$):* Two contrasting sections.
  - *Ternary Form ($ABA$):* Three sections (Statement, Contrast, Recapitulation/Restatement).
  - *Rondo Form ($ABACA$):* Principal recurring theme ($A$) alternates with contrasting episodes ($B, C$).
  - *Sonata-Allegro Form:* Three core movements: **Exposition** (introduces subjects in contrasting keys) $\to$ **Development** (themes fragmented and modulated) $\to$ **Recapitulation** (both subjects restated in the tonic key).

---

# SECTION 3: AFRICAN TRADITIONAL MUSIC & ORGANOLOGY

topics.title: Characteristics and Organological Classification
topics.content:
- **Core Elements of African Music:**
  - **Polyrhythm:** The simultaneous performance of two or more conflicting rhythmic meters (e.g., 3 against 2).
  - **Call-and-Response:** Soloist sings an improvised melodic phrase (**Call**), answered by the choral ensemble with a fixed refain (**Response**).
  - **Syncopation:** Deliberately shifting musical accents to the weak or off-beats.
  - **Ostinato:** A persistently repeated rhythmic or melodic phrase forming the foundation of a performance.
- **The Hornbostel-Sachs Classification of African Instruments:**
  1. **Idiophones (Instruments whose solid body vibrates to produce sound without strings or membranes):**
     - Slit Wooden Drum (**Ekwe** of the Igbo).
     - Clapperless Iron Hand Bell (**Agogo** of the Yoruba, **Ogene** of the Igbo).
     - Beaded Gourd Rattle (**Sekere** of the Yoruba, **Ichaka** of the Igbo).
     - Wooden Xylophone (**Ngedegwu** of the Igbo, **Kundung** of the Birom).
     - Lamellophone / Thumb Piano (**Agidigbo** of the Yoruba, **Ubo-aka** of the Igbo, **Mbira**).
  2. **Membranophones (Instruments that produce sound via a tightly stretched vibrating skin/membrane):**
     - Hourglass Talking Drum (**Dundun / Gangan** of the Yoruba, squeezed under the armpit to change pitch, mimicking tonal language).
     - **Bata** Drums (conical, double-headed drums sacred to Sango, the Yoruba god of thunder).
     - **Sakara** Drum (circular clay-framed tambourine-like drum).
  3. **Chordophones (Instruments that produce sound through vibrating stretched strings):**
     - **Goje / Goge:** One-stringed bowed horsehair fiddle popular in Hausaland.
     - **Kora:** 21-string harp-lute played by Mandinka griots in West Africa.
     - Earth Bow / Musical Bow.
  4. **Aerophones (Wind instruments that produce sound through a vibrating column of air):**
     - **Kakaki:** Long, straight metal royal trumpet (up to 3 meters long) blown exclusively for Emirs and Sultans in Northern Nigeria.
     - **Algaita:** Double-reed wooden oboe-like instrument used in Hausa royal courts.
     - **Oja:** Small notched wooden transverse flute of the Igbo, used for praising masquerades and titled men.
     - Elephant Tusk Horns (**Odu** of the Igbo).

---

# SECTION 4: WESTERN & NIGERIAN MUSIC HISTORY

topics.title: Western Music Eras and Composers
topics.content:
- **Baroque Era (1600–1750):** Continuous basso continuo, terraced dynamics, complex polyphony, fugues, cantatas, and oratorios.
  - **Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750):** Master of polyphony and fugue; composed *The Well-Tempered Clavier*, *Brandenburg Concertos*.
  - **George Frideric Handel (1685–1759):** Master of English oratorios; composed ***The Messiah*** (famous for the *"Hallelujah Chorus"*).
- **Classical Era (1750–1820):** Homophonic texture (melody with chordal accompaniment), emotional restraint, balance, perfection of the Symphony and String Quartet.
  - **Franz Joseph Haydn (1732–1809):** "Father of the Symphony" and "Father of the String Quartet".
  - **Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791):** Child prodigy; composed operas (*The Magic Flute, The Marriage of Figaro*), symphonies (*No. 40, 41*), and requiems.
  - **Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827):** Bridge between Classical and Romantic eras; composed 9 epic symphonies despite progressive deafness (*Symphony No. 5, Symphony No. 9 "Choral"*).
- **Romantic Era (1820–1900):** Emotional passion, expressive freedom, virtuosity, programmatic music, nationalism. Master composers: **Frédéric Chopin** (piano), **Franz Schubert** (Lieder), **Pyotr Tchaikovsky** (ballets).

---

topics.title: Nigerian Art and Popular Music Traditions
topics.content:
- **Pioneers of Nigerian Art Music:**
  - **T.K.E. Phillips (1884–1969):** Organist at Cathedral Church of Christ, Lagos; universally known as the **"Father of Nigerian Church Music"**; published the foundational treatise *Yoruba Music* (1953), pioneering the harmonization of indigenous pentatonic melodies without violating native tonal inflections.
  - **Fela Sowande (1905–1987):** The most renowned African composer of Western art music; composed the celebrated ***African Suite for String Orchestra***, skillfully weaving indigenous Nigerian folk tunes into classical symphonic structures.
  - **Akin Euba (1935–2020):** Renowned musicologist who formulated the creative theory of **"African Pianism"** (a keyboard performance style treating the European grand piano as an African percussive instrument to replicate the rhythmic complexity of traditional drum batteries).
  - **Laz Ekwueme:** Renowned composer and choral conductor; pioneer of scholarly studies in African choral polyphony.
- **Pioneers of Nigerian Popular Music:**
  - **Highlife Music:** Originated in Ghana, fused with Nigerian palm-wine acoustic music and brass bands. Pioneers: **E.T. Mensah** ("King of Highlife"), **Dr. Victor Olaiya**, **Cardinal Rex Jim Lawson**, and **Chief Osita Osadebe**.
  - **Juju Music:** Originated in Lagos in the 1930s among Yoruba social clubs. Pioneers: **Tunde King**, **I.K. Dairo** (introduced the accordion and talking drum), **King Sunny Ade** (introduced the pedal steel guitar, synthesizers, and vibraphone), and **Chief Commander Ebenezer Obey** (developed the distinctive "Miliki" sound).
  - **Afrobeat:** Created in the late 1960s by **Fela Anikulapo-Kuti**; an explosive, polyrhythmic fusion of highlife, American funk (James Brown), jazz, and traditional Yoruba spiritual drumming, infused with radical anti-corruption socio-political protest lyrics.
  - **Fuji Music:** Developed in the late 1960s by **Dr. Sikiru Ayinde Barrister**; evolved directly from traditional Islamic **"Were" / "Ajiwere"** music (early morning wake-up chanting performed during Ramadan); devoid of Western guitars, driven solely by talking drums, sakara, and vocal improvisation; modernized by Ayinla Kollington and King Wasiu Ayinde Marshal (K1 De Ultimate).

---

name: Arabic
overview:
**Subject Code:** `ARA`  
**Total Questions in UTME:** 40 Questions  
**Time Target:** 25 – 27 Minutes  
**Maximum Scaled Score:** 100 Marks  
**Authoritative Reference:** Official JAMB IBASS Syllabus for Arabic  

---

## Overview & How JAMB Tests Arabic

In the UTME, Arabic is tested via **40 multiple-choice questions** grouped into four major segments:
1. **Comprehension & Translation (*al-Fahm wa at-Tarjamah*) (~10 Questions):** Reading unseen Modern Standard Arabic (*al-Fusha*) prose excerpts, answering textual questions, and accurate translation between Arabic and English.
2. **Grammar & Syntax (*an-Nahw*) (~14 Questions):** Parts of speech, nominal vs. verbal sentences, case endings (*al-I'rab*), modifiers (*Kana* and *Inna* families), prepositions, pronouns, and number-gender agreement (*al-'Adad wa al-Ma'dud*).
3. **Morphology (*as-Sarf*) (~8 Questions):** The triliteral root system, the 10 verb measures/forms (*Awzan al-Fi'l*), active and passive participles (*Ism al-Fa'il* and *Ism al-Maf'ul*), verbal nouns (*al-Masdar*), broken plurals (*Jam' at-Taksir*), and the diminutive (*at-Tasghir*).
4. **Literature & Appreciation (*al-Adab*) (~8 Questions):** Major literary periods (Pre-Islamic *Jahiliyyah*, Early Islamic, Umayyad, Abbasid, and Modern), famous poets and writers (Imru' al-Qays, Hassan ibn Thabit, al-Mutanabbi, Ahmad Shawqi, Naguib Mahfouz), and poetic genres.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Grammatical Traps in JAMB Arabic:**
> - Governance of *Inna* vs. *Kana*:
>   - **إِنَّ (Inna) and its sisters:** Make the subject **Mansub** (Accusative with Fathah) and keep the predicate **Marfu'** (Nominative with Dammah).
>   - **كَانَ (Kana) and its sisters:** Keep the subject **Marfu'** (Nominative with Dammah) and make the predicate **Mansub** (Accusative with Fathah).
> - Numbers 3 to 10 Rule: The numeral takes the **OPPOSITE GENDER** of the singular countable noun (*al-Ma'dud*), and the countable noun must be **Plural Majrur** (Genitive).

---

# SECTION 1: GRAMMAR AND SYNTAX (AN-NAHW)

strategies.title: Strategy 1
strategies.description: **Inna vs Kana Inversion:** *Inna* makes the subject **Mansub** (Fathah) and predicate **Marfu'** (Dammah); *Kana* makes the subject **Marfu'** (Dammah) and predicate **Mansub** (Fathah).

strategies.title: Strategy 2
strategies.description: **Numbers 3 to 10 Opposite Gender Rule:** For numbers 3–10, if the countable noun is masculine, choose the numeral with **Ta Marbutah** ($\text{ة}$); if feminine, choose the numeral without it!

strategies.title: Strategy 3
strategies.description: **Prince of Poets Title:** The official "Prince of Poets" (*Amir ash-Shu'ara'*) in modern Arabic literature is **Ahmad Shawqi**.

strategies.title: Strategy 4
strategies.description: **Poet of the Prophet:** The companion appointed as the official poet of Prophet Muhammad (SAW) was **Hassan ibn Thabit**.

strategies.title: Strategy 5
strategies.description: **Form X Verb Meaning:** A Form X verb on the pattern **اِسْتَفْعَلَ (Istaf'ala)** denotes *requesting, seeking, or asking* for something (e.g., *Istaghfara* = asked for forgiveness).

strategies.title: Strategy 6
strategies.description: **Sound Feminine Plural Accusative Exception:** In the Accusative case (*Nasb*), the sound feminine plural ending in $\text{ات}$ takes a **Kasrah**, NEVER a Fathah.

strategies.title: Strategy 7
strategies.description: **Jussive Case (*Jazm*) Restriction:** The Jussive case applies **strictly to imperfect verbs (*al-Fi'l al-Mudari'*)**, never to nouns.

strategies.title: Strategy 8
strategies.description: **Genitive Case (*Jarr*) Restriction:** The Genitive case applies **strictly to nouns**, never to verbs.

strategies.title: Strategy 9
strategies.description: **Arab Nobel Laureate in Literature:** The first and only Arab author to win the Nobel Prize in Literature is Egyptian novelist **Naguib Mahfouz** (1988).

strategies.title: Strategy 10
strategies.description: **Diminutive Pattern:** The standard morphological pattern for the diminutive (*at-Tasghir*) is **فُعَيْلٌ (Fu'ayl)**, turning *Rajul* into *Rujayl*.

topics.title: Sentence Structures & Components
topics.content:
- **Parts of Speech (*Aqsam al-Kalam*):**
  - **Al-Ism (Noun / Substantive):** Indicates a person, animal, place, or concept without reference to time (e.g., كِتَابٌ, رَجُلٌ). Recognized by Tanween, Alif-Lam ($\text{ال}$), or following a preposition.
  - **Al-Fi'l (Verb):** Indicates an action tied to time: Past (*al-Madi*), Present/Future (*al-Mudari'*), and Imperative (*al-Amr*).
  - **Al-Harf (Particle):** Word with no complete independent meaning except when joined with a noun or verb (e.g., فِي, مِنْ, عَلَى, إِلَى).
- **The Nominal Sentence (*al-Jumla al-Ismiyyah*):**
  - A sentence that begins with a noun.
  - Composed of two essential parts:
    1. **Al-Mubtada' (The Subject):** The definite noun about which information is given; naturally **Marfu' (مَرْفُوع)** with Dammah.
    2. **Al-Khabar (The Predicate):** The word or phrase that completes the meaning; naturally **Marfu' (مَرْفُوع)** with Dammah.
    $$\text{Example: } \text{الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدٌ} \quad (\text{"The student is hardworking"})$$
- **The Verbal Sentence (*al-Jumla al-Fi'liyyah*):**
  - A sentence that begins with a verb.
  - Standard constituent order: **Verb (*Fi'l*) $\to$ Subject Doer (*Fa'il*) $\to$ Direct Object (*Maf'ul bihi*)**.
  - The **Fa'il (Subject)** is ALWAYS **Marfu'** (Nominative).
  - The **Maf'ul bihi (Object)** is ALWAYS **Mansub** (Accusative with Fathah).
    $$\text{Example: } \text{كَتَبَ التِّلْمِيذُ الرِّسَالَةَ} \quad (\text{"The pupil wrote the letter"})$$

---

topics.title: Modifiers: Inna and Kana Families (An-Nawasikh)
topics.content:
- **Kana and its Sisters (*Kana wa Akhwatuha* — Verbs of Becoming/State):**
  - Enter a nominal sentence and modify the case endings:
    $$\text{Ismu Kana} \implies \mathbf{Marfu'}\text{ (Dammah)} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Khabaru Kana} \implies \mathbf{Mansub}\text{ (Fathah)}$$
  - *Members of the family:* كَانَ (was), أَصْبَحَ (became in the morning), أَمْسَى (became in the evening), ظَلَّ (remained/continued), بَاتَ (spent the night), صَارَ (became/transformed), لَيْسَ (is not/negation), مَازَالَ (still/continues).
    $$\text{Example: } \text{كَانَ الجَوُّ بَارِدًا} \quad (\text{"The weather was cold"})$$
- **Inna and its Sisters (*Inna wa Akhwatuha* — Particles of Emphasis):**
  - Enter a nominal sentence and reverse the effect of *Kana*:
    $$\text{Ismu Inna} \implies \mathbf{Mansub}\text{ (Fathah)} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Khabaru Inna} \implies \mathbf{Marfu'}\text{ (Dammah)}$$
  - *Members of the family:* إِنَّ (verily/certainly), أَنَّ (that), كَأَنَّ (as if / resembling), لَكِنَّ (but/however), لَيْتَ (if only / wishful longing), لَعَلَّ (perhaps / hopeful expectation).
    $$\text{Example: } \text{إِنَّ اللهَ غَفُورٌ} \quad (\text{"Verily, Allah is Forgiving"})$$

---

topics.title: The Four Grammatical Cases (Al-I'rab)
topics.content:
| Case | Arabic Term | Primary Marker (Singular) | Dual Marker (*al-Muthanna*) | Sound Masc. Plural (*Jam' Mudhakkar*) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nominative** | **Ar-Raf' (الرَّفْع)** | **Dammah ($\text{ُ}$)** | **انِ** (*-ani*) | **ونَ** (*-una*) |
| **Accusative** | **An-Nasb (النَّصْب)** | **Fathah ($\text{َ}$)** | **يْنِ** (*-ayni*) | **ينَ** (*-ina*) |
| **Genitive** | **Al-Jarr (الجَرّ)** *(Nouns only)* | **Kasrah ($\text{ِ}$)** | **يْنِ** (*-ayni*) | **ينَ** (*-ina*) |
| **Jussive** | **Al-Jazm (الجَزْم)** *(Verbs only)* | **Sukun ($\text{ْ}$)** | Deletion of Nun | Deletion of Nun |

- **Key Jarr Triggers:** Noun preceded by a preposition (*Harf Jarr*: فِي, مِنْ, إِلَى, عَنْ, عَلَى, بِـ, لِـ, كَـ) OR functioning as the second noun in a possessive construct (**Mudaf Ilayhi**, e.g., كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ).
- **Sound Feminine Plural Exception:** Takes **Kasrah** instead of Fathah in the Accusative case (e.g., رَأَيْتُ الطَّالِبَاتِ).

---

topics.title: Number Systems & Countables (Al-'Adad wa al-Ma'dud)
topics.content:
- **Numbers 1 and 2:** Agree with the noun in gender, follow the noun as adjectives (e.g., رَجُلٌ وَاحِدٌ, اِمْرَأَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ).
- **Numbers 3 to 10 (The Gender Polarity Rule):**
  - The numeral takes the **OPPOSITE GENDER** of the singular form of the noun counted.
  - The counted noun (*al-Ma'dud*) is in the **Plural Genitive (Majrur)**:
    - *For Masculine Nouns (e.g., كِتَابٌ):* Use the feminine numeral (with Ta Marbutah):
      $$\mathbf{ثَلَاثَةُ\ كُتُبٍ} \quad (\text{Three books})$$
    - *For Feminine Nouns (e.g., غُرْفَةٌ):* Use the masculine numeral (without Ta Marbutah):
      $$\mathbf{ثَلَاثُ\ غُرَفٍ} \quad (\text{Three rooms})$$
- **Numbers 11 to 99:** The counted noun is ALWAYS **Singular Accusative (Mansub)**:
  $$\text{Example: } \text{إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ كَوْكَبًا} \quad (\text{"Eleven planets"})$$

---

# SECTION 2: MORPHOLOGY (AS-SARF)

topics.title: Triliteral Roots and Derived Verb Forms (Awzan al-Fi'l)
topics.content:
- Most Arabic words derive from a **3-consonant root (ف - ع - ل)**:
  - **Form I (فَعَلَ - Fa'ala):** Basic root action (e.g., كَتَبَ - wrote).
  - **Form II (فَعَّلَ - Fa''ala):** Causative or intensive action (e.g., عَلَّمَ - taught).
  - **Form III (فَاعَلَ - Fa'ala):** Mutual or reciprocal action (e.g., جَالَسَ - sat with).
  - **Form IV (أَفْعَلَ - Af'ala):** Transitive / causative (e.g., أَخْرَجَ - expelled / took out).
  - **Form V (تَفَعَّلَ - Tafa''ala):** Reflexive of Form II (e.g., تَعَلَّمَ - learned).
  - **Form VI (تَفَاعَلَ - Tafa'ala):** Mutual interaction between parties (e.g., تَعَاوَنَ - cooperated).
  - **Form VII (اِنْفَعَلَ - Infa'ala):** Passive/reflexive (e.g., اِنْكَسَرَ - broke / got broken).
  - **Form VIII (اِفْتَعَلَ - Ifta'ala):** Participatory / intensive (e.g., اِجْتَمَعَ - gathered / assembled).
  - **Form IX (اِفْعَلَّ - If'alla):** Colors and physical defects (e.g., اِحْمَرَّ - turned red / blushed).
  - **Form X (اِسْتَفْعَلَ - Istaf'ala):** Seeking, requesting, or considering (e.g., اِسْتَغْفَرَ - sought forgiveness).

---

topics.title: Derived Nouns, Participles, and Broken Plurals
topics.content:
- **Ism al-Fa'il (Active Participle / The Doer):**
  - Form I pattern: **فَاعِلٌ (Fa'il)** (e.g., كَاتِبٌ = writer, عَالِمٌ = scholar, جَالِسٌ = sitting).
  - Derived forms: Prefix $\text{مُـ}$ (*Mu-*) with Kasrah on penultimate letter (e.g., مُعَلِّمٌ = teacher, مُسْلِمٌ = Muslim).
- **Ism al-Maf'ul (Passive Participle / The Receiver of Action):**
  - Form I pattern: **مَفْعُولٌ (Maf'ul)** (e.g., مَكْتُوبٌ = written, مَعْلُومٌ = known).
  - Derived forms: Prefix $\text{مُـ}$ (*Mu-*) with Fathah on penultimate letter (e.g., مُعَلَّمٌ = taught).
- **Al-Masdar (Verbal Noun / Gerund):**
  - Name of the abstract action (e.g., كِتَابَةٌ = writing, خُرُوجٌ = exiting, اِسْتِغْفَارٌ = seeking pardon).
- **Jam' at-Taksir (Broken Plural):**
  - Irregular plurals formed by altering the vowel pattern of the singular noun:
    - كِتَابٌ $\to$ كُتُبٌ (Books)
    - مَدْرَسَةٌ $\to$ مَدَارِسُ (Schools)
    - قَلَمٌ $\to$ أَقْلَامٌ (Pens)
    - مَسْجِدٌ $\to$ مَسَاجِدُ (Mosques)
- **At-Tasghir (The Diminutive):**
  - Expresses smallness, affection, or contempt. Standard Form I pattern is **فُعَيْلٌ (Fu'ayl)**:
    - كَلْبٌ (dog) $\to$ كُلَيْبٌ (small puppy)
    - رَجُلٌ (man) $\to$ رُجَيْلٌ (little man)
    - قَلَمٌ (pen) $\to$ قُلَيْمٌ (small pencil)

---

# SECTION 3: OUTLINE OF ARABIC LITERATURE (AL-ADAB)

topics.title: Major Literary Epochs and Masterpieces
topics.content:
- **1. Pre-Islamic Era (*al-Asr al-Jahili*, c. 500 – 622 AD):**
  - Celebrated for oral poetry characterized by strict meter, monorhyme, desert imagery, and tribal valor.
  - **Al-Mu'allaqat (The Seven Suspended Odes):** Golden masterpieces written in gold ink and traditionally hung on the walls of the Ka'bah. Prominent poets:
    - **Imru' al-Qays:** The "Wandering King", master of love elegies (*Qifa nabki...*).
    - **'Antarah ibn Shaddad:** The valiant warrior-poet celebrated for heroic epics and chivalry (*Furusiyyah*).
    - **Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:** Known as the poet of peace and wisdom.
- **2. Early Islamic & Umayyad Era (622 – 750 AD):**
  - Language elevated by the inimitable eloquence of the Holy Qur'an (*I'jaz al-Qur'an*).
  - **Hassan ibn Thabit:** Officially titled the **"Poet of the Prophet"** (*Sha'ir an-Nabi*), defended Islam against Quraysh satires.
  - Umayyad court poets famous for poetic duel satire (*Naqa'id*): **Al-Farazdaq, Jarir, and al-Akhtal**.
- **3. The Abbasid Era (The Golden Age, 750 – 1258 AD):**
  - Blossomed in Baghdad; cosmopolitan, philosophical, scientific, and literary sophistication.
  - **Abu Nuwas:** Master of wine and urban hedonistic poetry.
  - **Al-Mutanabbi (Abu at-Tayyib):** Universally acknowledged as the greatest classical Arabic poet; celebrated for pride, philosophical mastery, and panegyrics for Sayf ad-Dawlah.
  - **Al-Jahiz:** Master of classical Arabic prose; author of *Kitab al-Hayawan* (The Book of Animals) and *Kitab al-Bukhala* (The Book of Misers).
  - **Al-Hariri:** Master of the *Maqamat* (picaresque rhymed prose tales).
- **4. The Modern Period (*an-Nahdah* — The Renaissance):**
  - **Ahmad Shawqi (1868–1932):** Egyptian neoclassical poet, crowned **"Prince of Poets"** (*Amir ash-Shu'ara'*).
  - **Hafiz Ibrahim:** The "Poet of the Nile".
  - **The Mahjar (Emigrant) Poets:** Arabic poets who emigrated to North and South America, establishing the Pen League (*ar-Rabitah al-Qalamiyyah*) led by **Kahlil Gibran** (*The Prophet*) and Mikha'il Nu'aymah.
  - **Naguib Mahfouz (1911–2006):** Egyptian novelist; won the **Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988** for his monumental *Cairo Trilogy*.

---

name: French
overview:
**Subject Code:** `FRN`  
**Total Questions in UTME:** 40 Questions  
**Time Target:** 25 – 27 Minutes  
**Maximum Scaled Score:** 100 Marks  
**Authoritative Reference:** Official JAMB IBASS Syllabus for French  

---

## Overview & How JAMB Tests French

In the UTME, French is tested via **40 multiple-choice questions** grouped into five main domains:
1. **Written Comprehension (~8 Questions):** Reading unseen contemporary narrative, descriptive, and journalistic passages in French, extracting factual information, and drawing inferences.
2. **Grammar and Sentence Structures (~18 Questions):** Articles, determiners, adjective agreement and placement, object pronouns (COD, COI, *y, en*), relative pronouns, verbal tenses (*Présent, Passé composé, Imparfait, Futur, Conditionnel, Subjonctif*), agreement of the past participle, and negative structures.
3. **Vocabulary, Idioms and False Friends (~6 Questions):** Everyday lexical fields, idiomatic expressions with *avoir* and *faire*, proverbs, and avoiding treacherous false friends (*faux amis*).
4. **Phonetics and Sound Discrimination (~4 Questions):** Nasal vowels, silent final consonants, liaisons, elisions, and rhyme matching.
5. **Francophone Culture and Civilization (~4 Questions):** Geography, national symbols, and culture of France and Francophone African countries bordering Nigeria (Benin, Niger, Cameroon, Chad, Togo, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Exam Distinctions in JAMB French:**
> - Agreement of Past Participle with *Avoir*: The past participle conjugated with *avoir* **NEVER agrees with the subject**, but **MUST agree in gender and number with a Preceding Direct Object (COD)** placed before the verb.
> - Passé Composé vs. Imparfait: **Passé Composé** expresses completed, specific, punctual actions in the past; **Imparfait** expresses ongoing, continuous past actions, habits, atmospheric descriptions, and emotional states.
> - Negative Transformation of Partitive Articles: In negative sentences, *du, de la, de l', des* change to simply **de / d'** (e.g., *Je mange du pain* $\to$ *Je ne mange pas de pain*).

---

# SECTION 1: GRAMMAR AND SENTENCE STRUCTURES

strategies.title: Strategy 1
strategies.description: **Agreement with Preceding COD (*Avoir*):** Look before the verb! In *Les lettres qu'il a écrites*, *lettres* is feminine plural placed before *avoir*, so the past participle must end with **-es**.

strategies.title: Strategy 2
strategies.description: **Negative Partitive Transformation:** After *ne... pas*, change *du, de la, des* to **de / d'**. E.g., *Je ne veux pas **de** sucre*.

strategies.title: Strategy 3
strategies.description: **Age Idiom Uses Avoir:** In French, you "have" years, you are not years old. The correct formulation is **J'ai 16 ans**, never *Je suis 16 ans*.

strategies.title: Strategy 4
strategies.description: **False Friend *Actuellement*:** *Actuellement* means **currently / at present**, NOT "actually".

strategies.title: Strategy 5
strategies.description: **False Friend *Librairie*:** A *librairie* is a **bookshop** where you purchase books; a *bibliothèque* is a public **library** where you borrow books.

strategies.title: Strategy 6
strategies.description: **Relative Pronoun Shortcut:** If the relative pronoun is immediately followed by a **VERB**, the answer is **QUI**. If followed by a **SUBJECT NOUN/PRONOUN**, the answer is **QUE (QU')**.

strategies.title: Strategy 7
strategies.description: **Weather Idiom Uses Faire:** For weather conditions, always use the verb *faire* (e.g., **Il fait beau**, **Il fait chaud**).

strategies.title: Strategy 8
strategies.description: **BANGS Adjectives Position:** Adjectives of Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness, and Size precede the noun (e.g., *un **beau** garçon*, *une **petite** maison*).

strategies.title: Strategy 9
strategies.description: **DR MRS VANDERTRAMP Verbs Take Être:** All movement verbs in this acronym use auxiliary **être** in the Passé Composé and their past participles **must agree with the subject**.

strategies.title: Strategy 10
strategies.description: **Pronouncing Liaison "S":** When a silent plural '-s' links to a vowel in liaison (*les enfants*), it is pronounced phonetically as a **[z]** sound.

topics.title: Articles and Adjective Rules
topics.content:
- **Articles & Partitives:**
  - *Definite:* **le** (masc.), **la** (fem.), **l'** (before vowel/silent h), **les** (plural).
  - *Indefinite:* **un** (masc.), **une** (fem.), **des** (plural).
  - *Partitive Articles (Expressing unspecified quantities):* **du** (masc.), **de la** (fem.), **de l'** (vowel), **des** (plural).
    $$\text{Positive: } \text{Elle boit du lait, de la bière et de l'eau.}$$
    $$\text{Negative Rule: } \mathbf{du, de\ la, de\ l', des} \xrightarrow{\text{negation}} \mathbf{de / d'}$$
    $$\text{Negative: } \text{Elle ne boit pas } \mathbf{de}\text{ lait, pas } \mathbf{de}\text{ bière, pas } \mathbf{d'}\text{eau.}$$
- **Placement of Adjectives (The BANGS Rule):**
  - Most French adjectives are placed **AFTER the noun** (especially colors, shapes, nationalities, and participles).
  - However, **BANGS adjectives precede the noun**:
    - **B = Beauty:** *beau, joli*
    - **A = Age:** *jeune, vieux, nouveau*
    - **N = Number / Rank:** *premier, deuxième, dernier*
    - **G = Goodness:** *bon, mauvais, gentil*
    - **S = Size:** *grand, petit, gros, long, haut*
    $$\text{Example: } \text{Un } \mathbf{grand}\text{ homme } (\text{before}) \quad \text{vs.} \quad \text{Une voiture } \mathbf{noire}\text{ et } \mathbf{ronde}\text{ (after)}$$
  - *Special Forms before Masculine Nouns starting with a vowel:*
    - *Beau* becomes **bel** (e.g., *un bel homme*).
    - *Vieux* becomes **vieil** (e.g., *un vieil arbre*).
    - *Nouveau* becomes **nouvel** (e.g., *un nouvel appartement*).

---

topics.title: Personal, Adverbial, and Relative Pronouns
topics.content:
- **Direct Object Pronouns (COD — Answers "Whom?" or "What?"):**
  - *me, te, le (him/it), la (her/it), nous, vous, les (them)*.
  - Placed **before the conjugated verb**:
    $$\text{Tu regardes la télévision? } \to \text{Oui, je } \mathbf{la}\text{ regarde.}$$
- **Indirect Object Pronouns (COI — Answers "To whom?"):**
  - Replaces *à + person*: *me, te, lui (to him/to her), nous, vous, leur (to them)*.
    $$\text{Il parle à sa mère? } \to \text{Oui, il } \mathbf{lui}\text{ parle.}$$
    $$\text{Il écrit à ses parents? } \to \text{Oui, il } \mathbf{leur}\text{ écrit.}$$
- **Adverbial Pronouns (Y and EN):**
  - **Y:** Replaces **à / dans / sur / en + place or inanimate object**:
    $$\text{Tu vas à Paris? } \to \text{Oui, j'}\mathbf{y}\text{ vais.}$$
  - **EN:** Replaces **de + noun**, a partitive article, or an expression of quantity:
    $$\text{Tu veux du café? } \to \text{Oui, j'}\mathbf{en}\text{ veux.}$$
    $$\text{Tu as trois frères? } \to \text{Oui, j'}\mathbf{en}\text{ ai trois.}$$
- **Relative Pronouns (Qui, Que, Dont, Où):**
  - **QUI:** Subject of the relative clause; **always followed by a VERB**:
    $$\text{L'homme } \mathbf{qui}\text{ parle est mon père.}$$
  - **QUE (QU'):** Direct object; **always followed by a SUBJECT + VERB**:
    $$\text{Le livre } \mathbf{que}\text{ tu lis est intéressant.}$$
  - **DONT:** Replaces a noun preceded by **de** (verbs like *parler de, avoir besoin de, avoir peur de*):
    $$\text{Voici la fille } \mathbf{dont}\text{ je t'ai parlé.}$$
  - **OÙ:** Indicates physical place or point in time:
    $$\text{La ville } \mathbf{où}\text{ j'habite...} \quad / \quad \text{Le jour } \mathbf{où}\text{ il est né...}$$

---

topics.title: Verbal Tenses and Agreement Rules
topics.content:
- **Passé Composé vs. Imparfait:**
  - *Passé Composé:* Expresses completed, punctual, historical events that occurred at a specific moment:
    $$\text{Hier, j'ai fini mes devoirs.}$$
  - *Imparfait:* Expresses habits, repeated past routines, physical/emotional descriptions, weather, and ongoing background actions:
    $$\text{Quand j'étais petit, je jouais au football tous les jours.}$$
- **Verbs Taking Être in the Passé Composé (DR MRS VANDERTRAMP):**
  - *Devenir, Revenir, Monter, Rester, Sortir, Venir, Aller, Naître, Descendre, Entrer, Rentrer, Tomber, Retourner, Arriver, Mourir, Partir* + **ALL Reflexive / Pronominal Verbs** (*se laver, se lever*).
  - Past participle **agrees with the subject in gender and number**:
    $$\text{Elle est } \mathbf{allée}\text{ à l'école. } (\text{feminine } +e)$$
    $$\text{Ils sont } \mathbf{partis}\text{ hier. } (\text{masculine plural } +s)$$
    $$\text{Elles sont } \mathbf{venues}\text{. } (\text{feminine plural } +es)$$
- **Agreement of Past Participle with Avoir (*L'accord avec Avoir*):**
  - The past participle conjugated with *avoir* agrees with the **PRECEDING DIRECT OBJECT (COD)** if placed before the auxiliary:
    $$\text{J'ai acheté les mangues. } \to \text{Les mangues que j'ai } \mathbf{achetées}\text{ sont sucrées.}$$
    $$\text{Voici ma nouvelle montre; mon père me l'a } \mathbf{donnée}\text{.}$$
- **The Subjunctive Mood (*Le Subjonctif*):**
  - Expresses subjectivity, doubt, emotion, obligation, and desire; introduced by conjunction **que**:
    - *Necessity:* **Il faut que** tu viennes.
    - *Desire:* **Je veux que** vous fassiez vos devoirs.
    - *Emotion:* **Je suis content que** tu sois là.

---

# SECTION 2: VOCABULARY, IDIOMS & FALSE FRIENDS

topics.title: Essential Idiomatic Expressions with Avoir and Faire
topics.content:
- **Expressions with Avoir:**
  - *Avoir faim* (To be hungry) | *Avoir soif* (To be thirsty)
  - *Avoir chaud* (To be warm/hot) | *Avoir froid* (To be cold)
  - *Avoir peur (de)* (To be afraid of)
  - *Avoir sommeil* (To be sleepy)
  - *Avoir raison* (To be right) | *Avoir tort* (To be wrong)
  - *Avoir l'air (de)* (To look/seem like)
  - *Avoir besoin de* (To need / to have need of)
  - *Avoir envie de* (To feel like / fancy doing something)
  - *Avoir ... ans* (To be ... years old — e.g., *J'ai 16 ans*, NOT *Je suis 16 ans!*)
- **Expressions with Faire:**
  - *Faire beau / mauvais* (To be good/bad weather)
  - *Faire chaud / froid* (To be hot/cold weather)
  - *Faire attention* (To pay attention / be careful)
  - *Faire la queue* (To stand in a queue / line up)

---

topics.title: False Friends (Les Faux Amis)
topics.content:
French words that resemble English words but possess completely different meanings:
| French Word | Common Mistaken Meaning | **Actual True English Meaning** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Actuellement** | Actually | **Currently / At present** |
| **Attendre** | To attend | **To wait for** (*Assister à* = to attend) |
| **Blesser** | To bless | **To injure / wound** (*Bénir* = to bless) |
| **Demander** | To demand | **To ask / request** (*Exiger* = to demand) |
| **Librairie** | Library | **Bookshop / Bookstore** (*Bibliothèque* = library) |
| **Monnaie** | Money | **Loose change / coins** (*Argent* = money) |
| **Rester** | To rest | **To stay / remain** (*Se reposer* = to rest) |
| **Journée** | Journey | **Full day / daytime** (*Voyage* = journey) |
| **Formidable** | Formidable / threatening | **Wonderful / Great / Terrific** |

---

# SECTION 3: PHONETICS, PRONUNCIATION & CULTURE

topics.title: Phonetics and Silent Letters
topics.content:
- **Nasal Vowels:**
  - [*ã*] spelled: *an, am, en, em* (e.g., *enfant, champ, temps*).
  - [*õ*] spelled: *on, om* (e.g., *bonbon, ombre*).
  - [*ɛ̃*] spelled: *in, im, ain, aim, ein* (e.g., *matin, pain, faim, plein*).
- **Silent Final Consonants (The "Careful" Rule):**
  - In French, final consonants (*-d, -p, -s, -t, -x, -z*) are **SILENT** (e.g., *chaud, trop, français, petit, nez*).
  - **Exceptions (The CRFL rule):** Final consonants **C, R, F, L** are usually **PRONOUNCED** (e.g., *sa**c**, ave**c**, me**r**, acti**f**, chefa**l**, bébi**l**).
- **Liaison:** Linking the normally silent final consonant of a word to the initial vowel of the following word:
  - *Les amis* is pronounced as **/le-za-mi/** (the silent 's' sounds like 'z').
  - *Un grand homme* is pronounced as **/un gran-to-me/** (final 'd' sounds like 't').

topics.title: Francophone Culture and Civilization
topics.content:

name: Hausa
overview:
**Subject Code:** `HAU`  
**Total Questions in UTME:** 40 Questions  
**Time Target:** 25 – 27 Minutes  
**Maximum Scaled Score:** 100 Marks  
**Authoritative Reference:** Official JAMB IBASS Syllabus for Hausa  

---

## Overview & How JAMB Tests Hausa

In the UTME, Hausa is tested via **40 multiple-choice questions** grouped into three canonical areas:
1. **Harshe da Nahawu (Language, Phonology & Grammar) (~16 Questions):** Karatun fahimta (reading comprehension), qa'idojin rubutu (orthography and punctuation), tsarin sauti (vowels, special hook consonants, tone system), nahawu (parts of speech, gender, pluralization, affixation), and translation.
2. **Adabi (Oral & Written Literature) (~14 Questions):** Adabin baka (tatsuniya, karin magana, habaici, ka-ci-ci-ka-ci, wake-wake) and rubutaccen adabi (analysis of classic and prescribed novels like *Magana Jari Ce*, *Shehu Umar*, *Ruwan Bagaja*, drama, and poetry).
3. **Al'adu da Gargajiya (Culture & Traditional Customs) (~10 Questions):** Life cycle ceremonies (haihuwa da rada suna, aure, jana'iza), sarautun gargajiya (the Emirate administrative hierarchy: Sarki, Waziri, Madawaki, Galadima), sana'o'in gargajiya (traditional crafts: rini, kira, dukanci, noma), and cultural festivals (Hawan Daba, Kalankuwa).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Key Exam Characteristics for JAMB Hausa:**
> - Special Hook Consonants (*Haruffan baki masu lankwasa*): **ɓ (implosive bilabial), ɗ (implosive alveolar), ƙ (ejective velar)**, alongside **ts (ejective alveolar affricate)** and **'y (glottalized palatal)**.
> - Prescribed Classic Literature Milestones: The 1933 Translation Bureau competition: *Ruwan Bagaja* (Abubakar Imam), *Shehu Umar* (Abubakar Tafawa Balewa), *Gandoki* (Muhammadu Bello Kagara), and *Magana Jari Ce*.
> - Traditional Occupations: **Rini** (dyeing indigo cloth in dye-pits e.g. Kofar Mata in Kano); **Dukanci** (leatherworking); **Kira** (blacksmithing); **Fawa** (butchery).

---

# SECTION 1: HARSHE DA NAHAWU (LANGUAGE & GRAMMAR)

strategies.title: Strategy 1
strategies.description: **Identify the 5 Hook Letters:** Remember the special Hausa hook consonants: **ɓ, ɗ, ƙ**, plus **ts** and **'y**.

strategies.title: Strategy 2
strategies.description: **Magana Jari Ce Author:** The monumental three-volume storybook *Magana Jari Ce* and *Ruwan Bagaja* were written by **Alhaji Abubakar Imam**.

strategies.title: Strategy 3
strategies.description: **Shehu Umar Author:** The classic novel *Shehu Umar* was authored by Nigeria's first Prime Minister, **Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa**.

strategies.title: Strategy 4
strategies.description: **Dan Maraya Jos Instrument:** The celebrated bard Dan Maraya Jos performed exclusively with the **Kuntigi** (one-stringed lute), NOT a drum.

strategies.title: Strategy 5
strategies.description: **Kofar Mata Pits Location:** The historic ancient indigo dye pits (*Rini*) celebrated across West Africa are located at **Kofar Mata in Kano**.

strategies.title: Strategy 6
strategies.description: **Naming Ceremony Day:** The traditional naming ceremony (*Rada Suna*) in Hausa custom is observed on the **7th day** after birth.

strategies.title: Strategy 7
strategies.description: **Emirate Army Commander Title:** The Commander-in-Chief of the cavalry and armed forces in the Hausa Emirate hierarchy is the **Madawaki**.

strategies.title: Strategy 8
strategies.description: **Tatsuniya Formula Openings:** Every Hausa folktale opens with *"Ga ta ga ta nan"* and closes with *"Kunkurus kan kusu"*.

strategies.title: Strategy 9
strategies.description: **Central Character in Tatsuniya:** The master trickster and cunning character in Hausa folktales is **Gizo** (the spider).

strategies.title: Strategy 10
